title: karma — the Isha Upanishad as a life
hook: the Isha's last verses: a life of work, and at the end, the mind told to remember what was done
carry: karma — the Isha Upanishad as a life
tomorrow: bhakti — the Narada Bhakti Sutras opening

segments.voice: Yesterday: karma, and the Isha Upanishad read as a guide for a working life. Eighteen short verses about how to act in a world that isn't yours to own. What did you do yesterday without grabbing at the result? Day six hundred ninety-two.

A golden lid. That's the picture the Isha Upanishad reaches for near its end. The face of truth, it says, is covered by a golden disc, and the speaker asks the sun, called here Pushan, the nourisher, to lift it. Then comes a short, startling verse. Let the breath go to the wind. Let this body end in ashes. And then the speaker turns, not to the gods, but to their own mind, and gives it one job. Today, the last of our three days with the Isha: how a life of karma ends.
screen: `A GOLDEN LID ON TRUTH'S FACE.` → `LET THE BODY END IN ASHES.` → `ONE JOB FOR THE MIND.`

segments.voice: The verse is seventeen of eighteen. In Sanskrit its heart is two words, repeated: kratu smara, krtam smara. Mind, remember. Remember what was done. Said twice, the way you'd repeat something important to someone half asleep. Now look at that word, krtam, what was done. It grows from the root kr, to do, and so does karma. Karma's first meaning is simply action, in the oldest texts especially the action of the sacrifice. Many scholars see the teaching of deeds bearing fruit across lives as growing on top of that plain meaning, while many Hindus hold it as part of the teaching from the start. So at the end of the Isha, the mind isn't asked to recite a creed or review its luck. It's asked to look at its karma in the plainest sense: the things this person actually did. Shankara, in his commentary, hears these lines as spoken by someone at the end of a life spent in work and meditation. The final verse is addressed to Agni, the fire, the god who knows all the ways. Lead us by a good path, it asks, keep crooked wrongdoing away from us, and it promises praise. That verse is older than the Upanishad: it appears in the Rig Veda too. Put the Isha together and it reads like a whole life. It opens by saying everything is wrapped in the Lord, so enjoy by letting go. In the middle it says to go on doing your work, even for a hundred years. And it closes here, with a body returning to ash, a fire asked for a good road, and a mind asked to remember what it did.
screen: `KRATU SMARA: MIND, REMEMBER.` · `KARMA AND KRTAM: ONE ROOT, TO DO.` · `AGNI, LEAD US BY A GOOD PATH.` · `OPEN, MIDDLE, END: A WHOLE LIFE.` · then, large: `REMEMBER WHAT WAS DONE.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let the breath slow down. Now do what the verse asks, gently. Remember what was done today. Start from waking and walk forward: what you said, what you made, what you carried, whom you helped, what you left undone. Don't grade any of it. Just let each deed pass in front of you, the way a fire lights each thing in a room in turn. When you reach this moment, rest with the breath. The bell holds the time.
Karma. Action, from the root to do. At the Isha's close the mind is told: remember what was done.

howItsDone: Many Hindus recite the Isha Upanishad whole, beginning and ending with its peace chant; its closing verses, including the prayer to Agni, are also heard in some funeral and remembrance settings. Karma yoga is lived as ordinary work done with care and offered without grasping at its fruit.

fork.setup: the body is returning to ash and the breath to the wind. the Isha gives the mind one last job. what is it?
options: ask for a better next life.
fork.reveal: kratu smara, krtam smara: mind, remember; remember what was done. said twice, like a last instruction.

original.note: Sanskrit karman, action, from the root kṛ, to do; the Isha's kṛtam, what was done, comes from the same root.

trapdoor: what you thought: karma is cosmic payback.
what it means: first of all it means action, the things a person actually does.
what a scholar hears: kṛtaṃ smara in Isha 17 shares karma's root kṛ; the last verse, to Agni, also appears in the Rig Veda.
